1:
The leave to speak comes from Agrippa, not from the governor who convened the court. Gill notes that it follows Festus's speech introducing the case, and Robertson presses the wording, literally it is permitted thee, as though Agrippa were master of ceremonies rather than Festus. Henry accounts for it by rank: Agrippa was the most honourable person present, bearing the title of king though holding only the power of other governors under the emperor, and senior to Festus though not his superior. He marks the silence that preceded it, since those are not the most forward to speak who are best prepared to speak and speak best; Paul needed no advocate, no Tertullus, and did not plead his appeal to Caesar as an excuse for silence, but embraced the chance of doing honour to the cause he suffered for.

The gesture is described by five voices. Barnes takes it for the usual posture of public speakers, the ancient statues being made with the right hand extended, which the robe clasped at the right shoulder left free. Clarke denies it was a rhetorical flourish, taking it for a bid for attention, and reconstructs the attitude down to the left hand under the cloak and the third and fourth fingers clenched, while Wesley and Ellicott put the chain into the picture. Ellicott notes that an arm, probably the left, was fastened to the guard; Wesley that the hand was stretched out chained as it was, a decent expression of Paul's earnestness. Robertson calls it a dramatic gesture with the chain still upon it, distinguishes it from the hand raised for silence earlier, reads the verb as an inchoative imperfect, and judges this the fullest of Paul's defences, without a word of censure, the apostle bearing the name of Christ before kings. Barnes sets out the aims, none of them release since the appeal was lodged: to vindicate his character and win Agrippa's attestation of it, to put the case correctly before the emperor as Festus wished, and to preach to the company.

The opening compliment is weighed carefully. Gill calls it a handsome and artificial way of gaining the king's affection, yet no mere compliment, since Lysias, Felix and Festus knew nothing of Jewish rites while Agrippa was master of them. Barnes adds that Paul could not flatter, though he would commend men as far as truth permitted. Ellicott finds a union of frankness and courtesy: Paul will not praise a prince whose character he must have known undeserving, but does recognise that Agrippa understood where Pharisee and Sadducee stood on the resurrection. Robertson reports Blass's observation that Paul, like Tertullus, opens with a compliment, but says only what he can truthfully speak. Calvin explains the strategy: Paul turns his defence into doctrine, and knowing that Festus set light by everything drawn from the law and the prophets he addresses the king, rejoicing that after speaking so long to deaf men he has at last a hearer able to judge aright; the request for patience follows from the commendation, since the more expert a man is in Scripture the more attentive he ought to be when religion is in question.

Ellicott takes customs in its half-technical sense as covering all the precepts of the Law; Wesley divides the pair, customs in practical matters and questions in speculative, noting that questions was Festus's own word, repeated and explained. Robertson glosses expert as a knower or connoisseur, notes that Agrippa had charge of the temple, the appointment of the high priest and the sacred vestments, and reports the difficulty of the accusative following, which Knowling calls an anacoluthon and Buttmann an accusative absolute. Wesley closes with an appraisal of the discourse: nothing could be imagined more graceful, the seriousness of the Christian, the boldness of the apostle and the politeness of the gentleman and the scholar appearing in a happy union.
4:
Calvin explains why the narrative begins so far back: Paul does not yet enter the cause, but having been burdened with many crimes he first avouches his innocence, lest hatred of the person prejudice the king against the doctrine; a sinister suspicion once lodged shuts up all the senses, so he drives away the clouds of evil opinion to be heard with purged ears. Robertson marks the same turn grammatically, the particles carrying Paul from exordium to statement of the case in a word found nowhere else in the New Testament. Barnes adds the history, that Paul was born in Tarsus but sent early to Jerusalem for schooling under Gamaliel, and that the commission against the Christians proves he was known to the men now accusing him. Clarke guesses he was sent up at about twelve, when male children were first brought to the yearly feasts; Ellicott restricts all the Jews to those of Judaea. Wesley catches the sting in the condition: they would not testify, knowing what weight his former life would add to his present witness.

On the strictest sect Clarke names the three, Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, the first reputed strictest in doctrine and practice. Ellicott prefers most rigid or most precise, the Greek having nothing to answer the English double superlative, and notes that sect is the word rendered heresy earlier in the book. Robertson calls it a true superlative, one of three such forms in the New Testament, and remarks that Paul had become a leading star of his party. Calvin reads the superlative against the grain: the sect was called strictest not for holiness of life but for sincerity of doctrine and learning, the Sadducees having fallen into gross ignorance by sticking to the letter and the Essenes caring little for doctrine.

What the hope of the promise means is the chapter's first real dispute. Clarke argues that it is the resurrection and not the Messiah, since the next verse says the tribes hope to attain to it, in the verb Paul uses of the resurrection in Philippians: the thing hoped for is something they come to, not something that comes to them, and the Messiah had come and gone already. Barnes joins the two, Paul believing the Messiah risen and therefore that the dead would rise. Ellicott takes the words for the whole expectation of a divine kingdom with Christ at its head; Robertson reports Page's view that these verses are a parenthesis, Paul's life in Christ being a development of the best in Pharisaism. Calvin presses the covenant itself, that Israel's adoption profited nothing without trust in the promised Mediator. Ellicott renders the twelve tribes as our twelve-tribed nation, observing that Paul, like James, assumes all twelve share one hope and ignores the legend of the lost ten, which Wesley meets by holding that a great part of them had returned from the east.

The closing question is not put to the king alone. Barnes notes the plural pronoun, finds no evidence that Agrippa doubted the resurrection though Festus and his company did, and observes that only an outline of a longer argument survives. Gill takes the address to be to heathens and Sadducees, and suspects Agrippa himself of Sadducean leanings; Ellicott reaches the same suspicion from another direction, the king being allied with the Sadducean high priests he had nominated himself. Robertson has Paul turning to an audience largely Gentile who scouted the doctrine as the Athenians had. Clarke reports the punctuation that makes the sentence an exclamation, and adds that two attributes stand pledged, God's truth for the promise and his power for the performance. Calvin ends there: nothing sinks less easily into men's brains than that bodies once consumed shall be restored, so Paul recalls them to the power of God, men being injurious to him who will not let his arm reach beyond their own reason.
9:
Gill hears the verse as a correction of the question just asked, since Paul could not wonder at an unbelief that had once been his own settled judgment. Barnes makes it the hinge of the defence: the confession of a violent and conscientious opposition shows that a man may be conscientious in enormous wickedness, and that almost all cruel persecution has gone on under the plea of conscience; conscience having driven him one way, only a demonstration as strong could have turned him. Robertson agrees that duty drove him on even in this sin, a common failing in persecutors. Ellicott catches a different tone, of sympathy and hope: one led himself from unbelief to faith would not despair of the like in others, even in Agrippa. Wesley dates it to Paul's years as a Pharisee. Calvin argues from the abruptness that Luke has abridged, the speech not hanging together unless Paul spoke of the grace and office of Christ between the covenant and this; the conversion is rehearsed to prove a commandment from heaven, since a man made a sheep of a wolf against his expectation, persuaded by no mortal, is plainly tamed by the hand of God, whereas one bred in the faith would have been sure of his calling without others knowing it.

The particulars follow. Gill sets them in Jerusalem, where Paul consented to Stephen's death and held the witnesses' clothes. Robertson glosses the verb for imprisoning as shutting a trapdoor, calls Paul the official persecutor under the Sanhedrin's direction, and notes that he names the chief priests, Sadducees, though himself a Pharisee. Ellicott finds courage in the word saints, Paul calling them before Agrippa the holy ones of Israel, what the Chasidim had been in an earlier generation. Whether others died beside Stephen is disputed: Barnes notes that the history records no other but sees no improbability in it, Clarke reads the verse as implying others unnamed, and Ellicott thinks that the likelier account, since Paul was breathing an atmosphere of slaughter. The vote divides them further. Robertson takes it literally, I cast down my pebble, a black one where the Greeks used white for acquittal, and follows the consequence that Paul sat in the Sanhedrin and was married then. Ellicott agrees that he belonged to that court or a delegated tribunal; Barnes denies it, rendering the phrase as joining with those who condemned; Wesley suggests the chief priests may have given him a vote for the occasion.

On the compelling to blaspheme the grammar carries the argument. Ellicott points out that the verb is imperfect and may express incomplete as well as continued action, so it need not follow that any yielded; Robertson calls it a conative imperfect and finds room to hope Paul did not succeed, though he elsewhere owns that he brought many unto death, and draws the hunting metaphor out of the verb for persecuting, a grand heresy hunt. Calvin will not soften it, taking the participle to mean that he did compel many, and inferring great corruption among the first believers, who under fear or stripes not only denied their Lord but spoke evil of his name. Barnes and Clarke seize on the madness: none but a madman persecutes men for their opinions, and the fiercest persecutor is the most furious madman of all; Ellicott adds that Paul pleads not only ignorance but the temporary insanity of fanaticism. Calvin makes the confession the point: Paul willingly utters his shame so the mercy of God may appear, condemning as madness the zeal for which others honoured him, and turning this against men ashamed to own an offence of ignorance who paint what they ought to weep over. Of the strange cities Clarke says they lay outside Jewish jurisdiction, Ellicott that Damascus was no solitary instance and the persecution may have raged through Samaria and Galilee, Robertson that Paul planned others beyond Palestine.
12:
Gill places the errand at Damascus, where Paul knew many believers had settled after fleeing Jerusalem. Ellicott divides the warrant into the general power delegated and the specific work for which Paul was answerable; Robertson notes that the second word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. Henry presses how little the change owed to anything in Paul: he was in the full career of his sin, his fury neither spent nor tired, holding as ample a commission from the chief priests as ever when a superior power obliged him to surrender it and take another to preach up the faith he came to suppress. Clarke, Barnes and Wesley alike decline to expound the story again, referring the reader to the ninth chapter.

Gill observes that the hour is a circumstance the earlier accounts omit, and that Paul names the king here to fix his attention; Wesley adds that the light's outshining the sun is no marvel, the created sun being nothing to the Sun of righteousness itself. Robertson notes that the comparison with the sun stands alone among the three accounts, marking the light as supernatural, and that Luke makes no attempt to harmonise their phrasing, Paul himself blending what Christ said directly with what came through Ananias. Henry turns the circumstances into an argument against delusion: not by night but at midday, not in a house where tricks might be played but in the open road, and no fancy of Paul's since it shone round his companions, who all fell to the earth; and where God once made the thick darkness his pavilion, now that life and immortality are brought to light Christ appears in a great light. Calvin argues the same from the other side, that the narrative is told to show Agrippa this was no apparition nor a trance robbing the man of judgment, since one who fell for fear yet heard a plain voice, asked who spoke and understood the answer was not beside himself, and so did not rashly change his mind but obeyed a heavenly oracle rather than strive on against God.

On the voice they divide between the language and the proverb. Wesley observes that Paul was not then speaking Hebrew, and did not trouble to say so when he was, concluding that Christ used the tongue on earth and from heaven alike; Robertson infers the same from the other end, the note being natural here because Paul speaks Greek. On the goad Robertson reports that the saying is genuine here though absent from the earlier accounts, a common proverb found in Aeschylus, drawn from an ox which, being pricked, kicks and takes a severer wound; Blass sees in Paul's use of a Greek and Latin proverb before this audience a mark of his culture. Ellicott confirms the reading here. Henry reads the words as caution rather than threat, the convictions designed to affect Paul and not affront him, and dwells on the naming: Christ called him by name and repeated it, which would startle a man in a strange place where he thought nobody knew him, and claimed his followers' sufferings as his own, so that little did Paul think, trampling on those he counted the blemishes of the earth, that he insulted the glory of heaven. Gill records the difficulty that all here fall to the earth while the earlier account leaves the company standing. Cyril of Jerusalem goes past the narrative to the dispensation behind it, wondering that the Spirit confined the other apostles to a few epistles but granted the former persecutor fourteen, not because Peter or John was less but that the doctrine might be beyond question coming from the enemy; and he has Paul own that he did it in ignorance, thinking the preaching of Christ the destruction of the Law and not knowing that he came to fulfil it.
16:
All of them notice that what follows stands in neither earlier account. Barnes thinks many circumstances went unrecorded, and that Paul dwells on these because they carry his authority for preaching to the Gentiles, while Clarke supposes he detailed such particulars as each occasion required. Ellicott goes further, taking the fuller report to embody the substance of those visions by which his future was marked out. Gill reads the command to rise as more than bodily, a bidding to take heart, the appearance being for honour, not destruction. Calvin says the same in his own key: Christ threw him down to humble him and now lifts him up, for whom he throws down he raises gently, coming not as an avenger for the stripes and bloody sentences but as a merciful Lord meaning to use the man's industry. Robertson notes that the reading makes Paul an eyewitness of the risen Christ, and gives Page's rendering of the passive future as the visions in which Christ would be seen by him.

The two titles are weighed. Clarke presses the first as an under-rower acting wholly under another's authority, so that Paul was to tug at the oar and bring the vessel through a tempestuous ocean to harbour; and the second as martyr, a word now reserved for those who testify at the hazard of their lives, as ancient history reports of Paul, beheaded at Rome by Nero. Barnes draws a ministerial rule from the same title: a preacher must witness not to what he can prove but to what he has felt in his own heart. On the promise of deliverance Robertson reports a real ambiguity, the verb rendered delivering being also used for choosing, with the papyri giving both and modern scholars divided. Ellicott sets the mission to the Gentiles here against the account tying it to the trance in the Temple three years later, siding with Galatians in dating it from the moment Christ was first revealed in him, and finds in the verb for sending the warrant of Paul's apostleship. Wesley marks the pronoun as the authority of the sender and the adverb as the date of the mission, his apostleship beginning with his conversion. Calvin observes what is not promised: Paul is armed against fear and made ready for the cross, but never told that those he benefits will receive him gladly, the world using the ministers of salvation as frantic men rail upon their physicians.

The commission itself is read as a summary of the gospel. Gill takes the opening of the eyes as the enlightening of the understanding, the Spirit's work throughout and ascribed to the apostle only as instrument. Calvin makes that his main labour: Paul might seem to take what belongs to God alone, but God transfers to his ministers the honour due to himself, not to lessen himself but to commend his Spirit's working, since he sends them out as no dead instruments or stage-players. He reads the verse as a key to the gate of heaven, inferring that since these things come by faith all men are naturally blind, bond-slaves of Satan and subject to death, and nothing is left to free will or merit. Barnes and Wesley trace the chain of blessings, Wesley remarking that he opens their eyes who sends Paul, and does it by the Paul he sends. Clarke argues from the word for forgiveness, which signifies the removal of sins, that purification and not pardon only is meant here. Ellicott notes that sanctified is a perfect, speaking of completed consecration rather than perfected holiness, and raises the construction of the closing words, which may go with either sanctified or receive; Robertson takes them with the participle; Calvin rejects the narrower reading, holding that the clause governs the whole period, so that by faith we come into possession of every good thing the gospel offers.
19:
The turn of the speech is a litotes. Robertson notes that the adverb gathers up everything said so far. Ellicott renders it strictly, I did not become disobedient, and finds the phrase significant for grace and freedom, the vessel of election constrained by the love of Christ retaining the possibility of disobedience. Wesley presses the point into doctrine, that having received power to obey he used it, so that even the grace which moved Paul was not irresistible. Calvin states its purpose, that Agrippa might see God was the author of all the Jews condemned as sacrilege and apostasy, and observes that Paul names the king because Festus and the Romans would not know what a heavenly vision meant.

Gill and Clarke follow the itinerary, Clarke reckoning three years at Damascus and in Arabia before the journey up to Jerusalem. Ellicott notes that the mention of the Gentiles after the region of Judaea points to work in Cilicia before Antioch, and divides the message into three stages, a repentance more than regret for consequences, a turning to God that implies faith and so justification, and works meet for repentance belonging to a progressive sanctification. Wesley puts the order shortly, that this repentance is previous to both inward and outward holiness; Calvin will not let the two be parted, conversion being joined to repentance so that we may know what repenting is, and those perverting the gospel who separate the grace of Christ from it.

On the seizure Clarke reduces the causes to four, the resurrection of the dead, the resurrection of the Christ whom they had slain, the claim that Jesus was Messiah, and the offer of salvation to Gentiles; Paul says nothing of defiling the temple or of disloyalty, his adversaries having dropped those charges at the previous hearing. Ellicott names one cause, that he taught the Gentiles they might claim every gift once reckoned Israel's prerogative. Calvin turns it against the accusers: had Paul offended they might have gone to law, where they far surpassed him in favour and authority, so their violence testifies they were destitute of reason. On the help acknowledged, Ellicott observes that the noun occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and describes the aid an ally gives a weaker friend. Barnes traces the deliverance past Lysias to God; Calvin adds that God reaches out his hand only where he acknowledges his minister, and that we are not spared to live idly. Robertson calls the perfect I stand a picture of Paul's stability.

The substance is put as two questions rather than two assertions. Robertson insists the verbal means not that the Christ must suffer but that he can, a form for capability found here alone in the New Testament; Ellicott says the same, recalling how slowly even the disciples received it, Peter's Be it far from thee expressing their first horror. Clarke reports the expedient by which the difficulty was met, two Messiahs, one of David to reign and one of Ephraim to suffer, a distinction with no foundation in the whole Bible. On the primacy in rising they agree in substance and differ in emphasis: Barnes denies it can be first in time, since Elijah and Christ himself had raised the dead, and makes it first in eminence; Clarke makes it a rising to die no more; Calvin says the word marks the cause rather than the order, Christ in rising becoming conqueror of death. Gill sets the sufferings in the human nature and refers them to the types and sacrifices; Calvin gathers under the word light all that belongs to perfect felicity, hearing in it Isaiah's promise that the people walking in darkness should see a great light. Ellicott ends on the order of the names, the sentence closing naturally at the prophets, Moses being added as an afterthought for hearers who, like the Sadducees, put the Pentateuch above them.
24:
Paul was still speaking when Festus broke in, and Robertson notes the linear present, thou art going mad. Henry weighs the manner, that Festus said it aloud and without consulting Agrippa, so that Paul should break off and the hearers be diverted, and judges it spoken not in anger so much as in scorn. What the much learning was they read differently. Ellicott takes the neuter plural strictly, thy many writings are turning thee to madness, the word being one the Jews used of their sacred books; Clarke thinks he meant only that a vast variety of knowledge had overcharged the brain, since Paul quotes none of the celebrated authors here as at Athens, but spoke of spiritual things a Roman heathen could not conceive. Henry finds the reproach double-edged, the fishermen apostles despised for having no learning and Paul, bred a Pharisee, for having too much; Barnes traces it to the earnestness and to the vision taken for delirium. Wesley turns it back: nay, Festus, it is thou that art beside thyself, for he saw that nature did not act in Paul, but the grace that acted in him he did not see. Calvin makes the outcry a case of truth trodden under foot by pride, Festus counting the man frenzied because the gospel is hidden from unbelievers, and refusing to attend lest he go mad himself.

The reply is admired by all. Clarke calls it the fullest proof of sound sense that could be given, and finds the two Greek words elegantly opposed, the apostle's soundness of mind against the governor's frenzy. Ellicott notes the union of calm protest with courtesy, and that the word for soberness was a favourite of the Greek moralists for the harmony of impulse and reason, so that Paul's enthusiasm had its root in truth, not madness. Barnes admires the turn by which, instead of defending his argument, Paul appeals to Agrippa and makes him the witness, which would tell on Festus more than any self-defence. Gill notes that the title of honour is given by custom, and Clarke that an apostle may address men in power in terms which taken literally imply more than they deserve; Henry draws the lesson that we are not to render railing for railing; Calvin that Paul does not vaunt his wit but is content with the plea that he teaches nothing but what is true and sober, truth set against fraud and sobriety against those thorny subtleties which are only seeds of contention. Wesley exclaims that mad men seldom call men by their names and titles of honour.

The appeal then passes over the governor's head. Wesley suspects that the very freedom of Paul's speech was itself one thing Festus took for madness. Barnes and Gill ground the appeal in Agrippa's long residence and his knowledge of the prophets, Barnes adding that it is evidence of honesty to declare everything without reserve before those able to detect an impostor. Robertson notes that the verb for the king's knowing is again a literary word; Clarke says the preaching, the passion and the resurrection were notorious, as the king's own answer shows. Ellicott makes the appeal twofold, to the prophets and to the communities that for a quarter of a century had rested on the belief that the Christ had come and risen, congregations as far as possible from an obscure sect lurking in corners. Henry adds that all the country rang of it, and that it shamed Festus to be ignorant of what Agrippa could not but know. Calvin sees the turn as deliberate, Paul going to the man in whom there was more hope and granting him the history only to call him back to the law and the prophets, since it was to small purpose to know what was done without knowing that the things foretold of Christ were fulfilled in the crucified Jesus.
27:
The question is put and answered in one breath. Gill refers it to what the prophets said of the sufferings and resurrection of Christ, and their fulfilment in Jesus. Barnes calls the address an instance of Paul's happy manner, meeting the charge of derangement with Agrippa's own testimony, and notes that Paul does not wait for the answer but anticipates it. Clarke sets out the inference the king was meant to draw: if the prophets spoke of a Messiah suffering and triumphing over death, and this was fulfilled in Jesus, the doctrine must be true. Robertson puts it as a trap sprung, since yes would place Agrippa in Paul's hands and no would deny the prophets; he slipped the coils with a touch of humour. Ellicott notes what the appeal opened: a Jew could not, before other Jews, speak of the Law and the Prophets as Festus had spoken of Paul's learning, so the argument from prophecy lay open. Wesley says only that Paul comes close to the heart.

What the king said is the chapter's hardest question. Clarke reads the words as the genuine effusion of a heart persuaded of the truth and kept from confessing it only by secular considerations, and cannot see how anyone could take them for irony; Barnes agrees, calling it a candid avowal and the crisis of Agrippa's life, since to be almost persuaded and go no further is the very position of guilt and danger. Wesley puts it in a sentence, that Festus was altogether a heathen and Paul altogether a Christian while Agrippa halted between; Gill allows the words might be serious or ironical and inclines to the former. Ellicott and Robertson deny that the Greek will bear the familiar rendering: the phrase means in or with a little, with little speech or labour or evidence. Ellicott takes the answer for a cynical sneer, evasive as well as derisive, noting that only Geneva among the older versions gives almost; Robertson judges the tone ironical but not unpleasant, the king pushing the appeal aside with a shrug. Calvin reports the same divided history, Valla translating it almost and the older interpreter leaving it word for word, and suggests it may be referred to time, as though Agrippa said Paul would make him a Christian in a moment; yet he does not dislike the sense almost, and reads the confession as wrung from a man who could resist the truth no longer.

Paul's reply is read by all as prayer rather than argument. Barnes and Gill mark it as a petition to God, since nothing but grace would overcome the heart's reluctance, and Wesley notes that Agrippa had spoken of being a Christian as a thing wholly in his own power, which Paul gently corrects by making it the gift and work of God. Robertson notes the courteous optative and renders the answering phrase both in little and in great, Paul taking the sarcasm kindly and saying only such as I am. Ellicott lays out three constructions and prefers the one keeping both conjunctions in their natural force, allowing that Paul may have caught up the phrase and given it a new sense. On the last words all of them stop. Clarke has the apostle lifting the chain, now detached from the soldier and wrapped about his own arm, and observes that the council could bear it no longer but rose at once and echoed his last word in their verdict, that he had done nothing worthy of death or of bonds. Ellicott hears an almost plaintive pathos in it, Paul content to keep his chains and leave them their thrones if only they might have what he had. Cyril of Jerusalem ascribes the whole to the Spirit: set amid the tribunals, before Felix at one time and Festus and Agrippa at another, Paul obtained a grace so great and triumphant in wisdom.
30:
The court breaks up without a word to the prisoner. Robertson notes that the verb agrees with the king alone, and remarks drily that the entertainment was over; Gill records that the opening clause is missing from the Alexandrian copy and from the Vulgate, Syriac and Ethiopic versions, and that they withdrew into an apartment adjoining the judgment hall. Ellicott reads the rising as a sign that the words had told, since they now felt this was no common criminal and no fomenter of sedition, and observes that Paul was treated from that time with more respect. Wesley looks the other way, calling it an unspeakably precious moment for Agrippa and leaving it there, whether he improved it being a thing to be seen in that day.

Robertson describes the conference next door as the eager talk of dignitaries about a wonderful speech, and presses the awkwardness of their conclusion: the verdict was unanimous among Romans, Jews and Greeks, and was what Festus had already said, which leaves the governor to explain why the man had not been freed long since; and he adds the sober note that Paul had won none of them to Christ. Barnes counts the witnesses instead, Lysias, Felix, Festus and Agrippa all concurring, so that the acquittal could not have been fuller. Ellicott explains why the historian dwells on it, the charge of lawless and revolutionary tendencies being too often brought against the apostle, and too current against his followers, to be passed over. Wesley will not let the verdict pass as a compliment, noting that they speak of the whole life and not one action, and asking whether nothing more could be learned from such a discourse, since a favourable judgment of such a preacher is not all God requires. Calvin turns it on Festus, who in agreeing with the rest condemns himself, having brought Paul into these straits by unjust dealing and endangered his life under colour of changing the place.

The last word belongs to the appeal. Gill notes that Agrippa gives his opinion by way of advice, the determination lying with the governor; Barnes takes the remark for a full declaration of the king's conviction and an instance of bold dealing ending well, the appeal to Agrippa's own belief having impressed rather than offended him. Robertson reads the sentence as a condition contrary to fact, so that Paul certainly could have been released, and judges that Festus comes out of it with no honour, though Agrippa was a favourite at court and might have moved him to write well of the case. Clarke says the king was prompted to wish an immediate release which the registered appeal had made impracticable, and reports Bishop Pearce's conjecture that Agrippa afterwards represented the case so favourably at Rome that Paul was soon at liberty there, which would explain the centurion's courtesy on the voyage. Ellicott finds in the decision a vindication of Paul's course, since the matter could now neither be hushed up nor disposed of by a release that would have exposed him to conspiracy, so that he gained at last the safe journey to the imperial city he had long desired. Calvin says the same from the other side, that though the appeal seems to have hindered him it was the only escape from death, and that Paul is content with it because matters were no longer entire and because the vision had told him he was called to Rome. Chrysostom presses the same providence further: they acquit as undeserving even of bonds the man they had just called mad, and would have released him but for the appeal; yet it was ordered so that he should go bound, for if his Lord was reckoned among the transgressors much more might he be, and the marvel is that one so mixed with such men should take no harm from them.
